questions.q: Pick the right sign-off for a letter to your cousin: Yours faithfully / Yours lovingly / Yours sincerely.
questions.a: 'Yours lovingly' (affectionately also fine) — personal relationship → personal subscription. A wrong answer 'faithfully' reveals the student memorized one pair and applies it universally — the pairing is relationship-indexed, not letter-indexed.

questions.q: Fix this informal opener: 'I am writing to apprise you of my recent academic achievement.'
questions.a: Something like 'You'll never guess — I topped the class!' A wrong answer merely removing contractions shows the student thinks informality is a surface feature — the real signal is communicative intent (sharing excitement), not grammar.

questions.q: Does an informal letter need a subject line?
questions.a: No — subject lines belong to formal/business formats. A wrong answer adding one shows the student hasn't separated the two skeletons and treats 'letter' as one format with optional parts.

questions.q: An informal letter keeps a lighter skeleton — sender's address, date, 'Dear [name]', conversational body, 'Yours lovingly/______' — and ADDS what formal letters ban: contractions, personal voice, questions to the reader, idioms.

Fill in the blank: An informal letter keeps a lighter skeleton — sender's address, date, 'Dear [name]', ______ body, 'Yours lovingly/affectionately' — and ADDS what formal letters ban: contractions, personal voice, questions to the reader, idioms.
Fill in the blank: Same ______ diagram, fewer blocks: no receiver's address, no subject.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student produces the informal skeleton correctly and sustains a warm, personal register — including choosing the correct salutation-subscription pair (Dear Rahul ↔ Yours lovingly) and writing a body that sounds like speech, not a report.
